title: Like a trumpeter
hook: a mind of kindness fills the first direction, then the second, third and fourth, above and below (DN 13)

segments.voice: Yesterday: indifference is not equanimity. Your line was care, then let go. Did you catch a shrug pretending to be calm? Day two hundred forty-two.

At dawn, someone stands at the edge of a village with a conch shell, takes one deep breath, and blows. The sound doesn't pick who hears it. It rolls out to the east, and the west, and the north and the south. The farmer hears it, the child hears it, the neighbor who doesn't like the conch blower hears it too. It takes no extra effort to reach one more house. That picture is in an old Buddhist text, and it's describing what a kind mind can do. Today: like a trumpeter.
screen: `A CONCH AT DAWN.` → `THE SOUND DOESN'T PICK.` → `LIKE A TRUMPETER.`

segments.voice: The text is the Tevijja Sutta, the one we opened ten days ago: two young brahmins, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, asking the Buddha the way to union with Brahma. He answers in their own terms. He describes a monk who lets his mind, full of kindness, pervade one direction, then the second, then the third, then the fourth. Then above, below, across, everywhere, the whole wide world, with a mind that is abundant, grown great, measureless, free of hatred and ill will. Then he gives the image. It's like a strong conch blower who makes himself heard in all four directions without any strain. In the same way, the text says, nothing is left out or passed over. And then the same sweep is repeated for compassion, for gladness, and for equanimity. Two things are worth noticing. First, the practice has an order. It doesn't start with everywhere. It starts with one direction and widens, the way sound travels outward from one breath. Second, the word measureless is the whole point. That's why these four are called the immeasurables. A kindness that stops at the edge of my people, or my street, has a measure. This one keeps going, the way the conch keeps sounding past the last house, until there's no edge left to stop at.
screen: `TWO BRAHMINS BRING A QUESTION.` · `ONE DIRECTION, THEN THE NEXT.` · `A HORN HEARD EVERYWHERE, WITHOUT STRAIN.` · `NOTHING LEFT OUT.` · then, large: `BOUNDLESS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Start with kindness, and send it one way, in front of you: whoever is out there, in that direction, may they be well. Then to your right. Behind you. To your left. Above, below. Then let it spread everywhere at once, like the sound of the conch. If you have time, do the same with compassion, then gladness, then equanimity, each one a little wave outward. No effort to reach anyone. The bell holds the time.
Like a trumpeter. The horn blower is heard in every direction without strain: a kind mind reaches everywhere, and nothing is left out.
Your line: boundless. Today, when you're out in the world, send one quiet good wish in each direction you face. No one has to know. Day two hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: In Buddhist communities this practice is called radiating or pervading the brahmaviharas: practitioners send kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity outward direction by direction, often after first wishing well to themselves and to people near them.

fork.setup: two young brahmins ask the Buddha how to reach union with Brahma. how does he answer?
options: he refuses to use their words at all.
he describes a mind of kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity filling every direction.
he tells them to study with a different teacher.
fork.reveal: he answers in their own terms, and describes the four immeasurables spreading everywhere, like a horn heard in every direction.

original.note: Pali appamaññā: the immeasurables, qualities with no measure or edge.

trapdoor: what you thought: a trumpeter is a musician showing off.
what it means: a horn heard everywhere without strain; kindness that leaves no one out.
what a scholar hears: the Pali saṅkhadhama is a conch blower; Rhys Davids rendered it 'trumpeter' in his 1899 Dialogues of the Buddha.

notes: The Tevijja Sutta is paraphrased; Rhys Davids's 1899 translation exists but was not quoted because the exact wording was not verified.

The sutta's frame (a dispute among brahmins about union with Brahma) is described neutrally; please check the tone is fair to the brahmin tradition.
